channel.title: Gnarly Void - geometric
channel.description: Tufted fiber art, weaving, pottery, and handmade objects by Jake Goldsborough in the Pacific Northwest.

item.title: Discourse
item.author: site@gnarlyvoid.com (Jake Goldsborough)
item.description:
A logo that lives on a screen, moved into a room.

This is the Discourse mark - the speech bubble made of nested colored arcs, red through blue, wrapped in a heavy black field. It's a shape I look at every day; Discourse is where I work. Tufting it is a small act of translation: taking something that exists as a vector on a login page and giving it pile, weight, and a wall to hang on.

The build is the good part, and it goes in from the inside out. The cream bubble first, then each color laid around it as its own ring - orange, red, green, blue - and finally the black poured in around the whole thing to make the field. The second image is the whole thing coming together, stage by stage. Watching a logo assemble in yarn is oddly satisfying; it's the same shape the whole way, just gaining substance.

The black surround does the heavy lifting. It's most of the piece by area and none of the interest, which is exactly its job - a flat dark field that makes the little rainbow of arcs sit forward and glow. Tufting that much black is a slog with no feedback; you're just filling, and the payoff only shows up once the last of the canvas disappears.

Software doesn't usually get to be a physical object. This one does now, on a wall, under warm light, being exactly what it always was and never could be.

item.title: Loaded II
item.author: site@gnarlyvoid.com (Jake Goldsborough)
item.description:
Every die needs a partner.

This is the black one - deep black pile, cream pips, dense foam core - the exact inverse of Loaded. Same scale, same cube, same Angine de Poitrine black-and-white world; the colors just trade places. Set the two together and they read as a pair before they read as dice: one dark, one light, stacked on the couch like they've always lived there.

The inversion changes how the pips work. On the cream die the black dots do the talking; here the cream pips are the only light in a field of black, so they carry more - little bright knots you find by eye and by hand. Tufting black-on-black for the body meant leaning entirely on form and shadow, since color gives you nothing.

Same honest core as its sibling: foam, not stuffing. Press in and it gives, then shoves back and keeps its corners. A cube wants edges, pile wants to round them off, and the foam holds the argument in the middle so the thing stays crisp across the room and soft under a hand.

Two dice now, black and white, waiting to be thrown. One was never going to be enough - a single die is a number, but a pair is a game.

item.title: Deck 001 & Deck 002
item.author: site@gnarlyvoid.com (Jake Goldsborough)
item.description:
Two decks for a show, tufted instead of painted.

These went into a group skateboard deck show at ADX Portland, the maker studio I'm a member of. The brief is the deck shape - that long rounded pill everyone knows - and what you do inside it is yours. I did what I always do: I reached for yarn instead of paint.

Deck 001, on the left, is monochrome and hard-edged - cream, grays, and black cut into arcs, blocks, and angular shards, a little cubist, a little Bauhaus. It's the more structural of the two: the composition does the work, and the palette stays out of its way.

Deck 002 is the opposite instinct. Vertical bands of cream, rust, orange, gold, and brown running the length of the deck, a warm sunset laid down in stripes. No drawing, just color doing all the talking - the earth-tone cousin of the traffic-light and Birdhaus pieces.

Same shape, two grammars: one that composes and one that glows. Hung side by side on the same wall, they read as a conversation - which is the fun of making two for one show instead of one.

A skateboard is built to be ridden and scuffed. These are built to be touched and hung. Same silhouette, opposite fate.

item.title: Loaded
item.author: site@gnarlyvoid.com (Jake Goldsborough)
item.description:
The oldest random number generator, rebuilt as an object with opinions.

A die at many times scale, tufted in deep cream pile with black pips over a dense foam core. Six up top, five on the face. The form could not be simpler - a cube and some circles - and that's what makes it work: dice are pure geometry with rules attached, and scaling one up in fiber keeps the geometry, the rules, and the game.

The piece is a nod to Angine de Poitrine, a band I love whose whole visual world runs on dice and black-and-white. This is that aesthetic made physical: monochrome, blunt, a little absurd, sitting on the couch like it owns the place.

The core is the honest part. Dense foam, not stuffing - press into the pile and the surface gives, but the cube pushes back and holds its corners. A cube asks for edges, pile wants to round everything off, and the foam is what lets both win: crisp enough to read as a die across the room, soft enough that reading it up close means touching it.

And it rolls. Underhand, across the floor, tumbling in slow motion and landing with a soft thud and a verdict. Every die promises a fair result; this one just takes its time delivering.

item.title: Drake
item.author: site@gnarlyvoid.com (Jake Goldsborough)
item.description:
The wing is carved. That changes everything.

Most tufted work earns its depth through pile alone; here the drake's wing rides over the body in sculpted relief, so the bird actually stands off the wall. Cream shoulder, brown coverts, the blue speculum flashing between black and white bars - the one part of a mallard that looks designed gets the most dimensional treatment.

Behind him the scene goes cubist: a red sun scored with black rules, gray-green bands of horizon, a ground plane shattered into blue and gray triangles. The bird is all field-guide fidelity - bottle-green head, white collar, chestnut breast, orange feet - standing in a landscape that gave up on realism entirely. He doesn't seem to mind.

A sculpted cream border traces the whole silhouette and squares it off, part frame, part halo, keeping the composition one object instead of a bird pasted on a backdrop.

Drake holds the tension between taxidermy and toy - anatomically earnest, structurally playful, a specimen mounted in a world made of shapes.

He's a piece in the Birdhaus series - forms over feathers - the red sun and its black bars carried from screen into pile.

item.title: Penrose
item.author: site@gnarlyvoid.com (Jake Goldsborough)
item.description:
An impossible object, made real.

The Penrose triangle only exists as a drawing - three beams that meet at right angles no physical object could hold. Tufting it is a small act of defiance: taking a shape that cannot exist and giving it high-pile texture, weight, and a place to hang on a wall.

The whole illusion rides on value. There's no trick geometry here, just three faces in light gray, mid gray, and near-black, and the eye does the rest - reading the gradient as light falling across surfaces that fold impossibly into each other. Flatten the color and the magic collapses; it's the tonal shift that keeps the beams turning.

Tufted with dense, even pile, the hard edges of the figure stay crisp while the surface goes soft and inviting. Precision holds the shape; texture makes you want to touch the thing your eyes insist can't be there.

Penrose is a study in contradiction - rigid and plush, flat and dimensional, impossible and hanging right in front of you.
